title: Home to the hills
hook: after battles with Mughal forces, Guru Hargobind settles at Kiratpur and spends his last years quietly

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloak with fifty-two tassels, and Bandi Chhor: the prisoners who walked out holding on. Your line was no one freed alone.

Some people never learn to stop. The firefighter who can't sit through dinner without listening for the siren. The parent who, years after the kids leave, still sleeps with one ear open. The soldier who comes home and can't find the off switch. Guru Hargobind spent most of his life on guard: a boy Guru after his father's killing, two swords, an army, a prison fort, and in his later years, real battles. Then he went up into the foothills and did something his whole life had not trained him for. He rested.
screen: `PEOPLE WHO NEVER STOP.` → `A LIFE ON GUARD.` → `THEN, THE FOOTHILLS.`

segments.voice: In the years around 1634, the peace between the Guru and the Mughal authorities broke down. Tradition tells of several clashes; one began, the story goes, with a dispute over a hunting hawk. Sikh accounts count four battles, in and around Amritsar and further south, and say that in each the Guru's small force held its own against much larger ones. Sikhs remember these as the first battles fought by a Guru. In one, the Guru's own youngest son, a boy named Tyag Mal, fought so hard he earned a new name; that's a story for day seventy-four. But the Guru did not want endless war. After the last battle, at Kartarpur near the Beas river, he led his family and followers north into the Shivalik foothills, to a town on the Sutlej river called Kiratpur. His son Baba Gurditta had founded it on land given by a hill raja. It was quiet, green, out of the way. There, tradition says, for about his last ten years, Guru Hargobind lived peacefully. He kept horses and a hunting ground, but the fighting was over. He preached, received visitors, looked after his community, and prepared the next Guru, passing over his sons to choose a grandson, Har Rai, a gentle boy of about fourteen. Guru Hargobind died at Kiratpur in 1644. The Guru who first wore two swords put them down. Sikhs read miri piri as a balance, not a call to fight forever, and at Kiratpur the balance tipped toward rest.
screen: `BATTLES AROUND 1634.` · `NORTH TO KIRATPUR.` · `TEN QUIET YEARS.` · `A GENTLE GRANDSON CHOSEN.` · then, large: `EVEN WARRIORS REST.`

segments.voice: Let this be the easiest sit of the week: lean back if you can, jaw loose, hands heavy, shoulders down from your ears. Think of what you've carried these last few days, and set each piece down, one at a time, like a weapon laid on a table. Nothing is guarding the gate right now; just rest.
Kiratpur. The town in the Shivalik foothills where Guru Hargobind spent his last ten years in peace, after years of battles.
Your line: even warriors rest. Tomorrow, a boy in that quiet garden. Day sixty-eight, and a rest well earned.

howItsDone: Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, where Guru Hargobind spent his last years, is a place of Sikh pilgrimage, and some Sikh families today take the ashes of their loved ones there to be scattered in the river.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS fix: Tyag Mal was Guru Hargobind's own youngest son, not 'a Sikh boy'; the garbled 'and the year a Sikh boy...' sentence rewritten. 'About his last ten years' at Kiratpur (c. 1635–1644); confirm. Kiratpur founded by Baba Gurditta c. 1626 on land from the Raja of Kahlur; confirm.
Har Rai's age at succession given as about fourteen (born 1630). Confirm.
